title: Design a ticket-booking system (like BookMyShow).
description: Seat inventory under contention: holds, idempotent checkout, overbooking prevention, and fair access during on-sale storms.

data.text: **Question:** Design a ticket-booking system where users browse shows and book specific seats under heavy on-sale load.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Browse cinemas/showtimes; view a seat map with live availability
Select specific seats and hold them during a short payment window
Never sell the same seat twice (no overbooking)
Booking is idempotent: retried payments don't double-book
Fair access at on-sale time: queue/rate-limit rather than melt
Cancellation/refunds release inventory correctly

data.caption: Booking flow: holds in Redis, authoritative seat state in SQL, async payment confirmation
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Client] --> B[API Gateway - auth, rate limit]
    B --> C[Showtime/Seat Service]
    C --> D[(Seat Inventory - SQL, row-locked)]
    C --> E[(Redis: active holds, TTL)]
    F[Payment Webhook] --> G[Booking Service]
    G --> D
    G --> E
    H[Hold Expiry Worker] --> D
    I[Queue at on-sale] --> J[Token Gate]
    J --> B

data.text: The design tension: seat state must be **authoritative and transactional** (SQL row locks), but the on-sale moment brings traffic a database can't absorb directly. The standard resolution is a **two-layer model**: a fast Redis layer for short-lived holds (TTL = payment window) and SQL as the source of truth, with the hold→confirm transition as a single locked transaction.

items: Seat row model: (showtime_id, seat_id) unique row with status (available/held/sold) — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on hold creation is the correctness backbone
Hold with TTL: Redis SET NX EX (seat:user, 600s); expiry worker (or lazy expiry) returns lapsed holds to available — Redis is an accelerator, SQL decides truth
Idempotency keys: client generates a booking id; payment webhook + client retries converge on one confirmation (unique constraint on booking id)
Overbooking defense: the confirm transaction re-verifies sold_count vs capacity inside the lock; allocation counters per showtime pre-partition contention
On-sale storm: virtual waiting room — a queue issues short-lived tokens; gateways admit token-holders only; per-user rate limits on hold attempts
Contention sharding: partition by showtime; a blockbuster show is one hot key — mitigate with per-section counters (rows A-J vs K-T) so locks don't serialize globally
Read path: seat maps are read-heavy — cache aggressively (CDN 5-10s), serve 'last known' with a staleness banner near on-sale time
Payment: authorize during hold, capture on confirm; on webhook timeout, GET the payment status instead of trusting either side's memory
Cancellation: refund via saga — payment refund step, then seat release; both idempotent, compensation logged

data.title: The double-booking bug lives in the gap
data.text: Classic failure: hold in Redis succeeds for two requests racing the same seat, both proceed to payment, both capture — then one confirm transaction fails and you owe a refund plus a customer's ruined evening. The confirm must re-check seat state under a row lock, and holds must be exclusive (atomic SET NX) — every step between must assume it can be retried.

rows: One row per seat per show; locked on hold/confirm

items: Redis loses the hold state — SQL remains authoritative; reconcile from bookings, not Redis
Payment captured but confirm crashed — idempotent confirm replays from the webhook
User abandons checkout — TTL expiry frees the seat; expiry worker must be exactly-once-ish (idempotent release)
Concurrent cancellations + expiry — double release guarded by status transitions (only HELD→AVAILABLE once)
Dynamic pricing mid-hold — price locked at hold creation, honored at confirm
Accessibility/companion seats requiring pairs — hold must be multi-seat atomic or reject

items.question: Why not pure Redis for seat state?
items.answer: Payments and inventory need durable, transactional truth with auditing. Redis accelerates holds; SQL row locks guarantee the invariant. On Redis loss, the system rebuilds holds from bookings — losing speed, never correctness.

items.question: How does the virtual waiting room work?
items.answer: At on-sale, all clients hit a queue service that issues position tokens; only token-holders reach the booking API at a controlled rate. Turns a thundering herd into a shaped stream; requires a fair, restartable queue and honest wait-position UX.

items.question: How do you prevent bots from eating the best seats?
items.answer: Rate limits per user/account/device, verified identity at high-demand on-sales, CAPTCHA at the gate, and purchase limits. A pure-technical defense loses to determined scalpers without identity signals.

items.question: What happens under a showtime data-center partition?
items.answer: Single-writer per showtime region; cross-region failover promotes the replica and reconciles in-flight bookings via the payment provider's authoritative status — idempotency keys make replay safe.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: SQL row locks are the overbooking defense; Redis holds are a TTL accelerator
Idempotency keys make payment retries and webhook replays converge
Virtual waiting room + rate limits turn on-sale herds into shaped traffic
Every transition (hold/confirm/release) must be idempotent and status-guarded
data.takeaway: Booking systems live or die on one invariant — a seat is sold exactly once — so put that invariant behind a row lock and make everything around it safely repeatable.
